names.name: buddha-nature, the essence of the sugatas (bde gshegs snying po)
the emptiness endowed with all supreme aspects (rnam kun mchog ldan gyi stong nyid)
Kālacakra, the primordial buddha (dus kyi 'khor lo, dang po'i sangs rgyas)

descriptions: permanent, stable, peaceful and eternal (rtag brtan ther zug g.yung drung)
endowed from the beginning with the inseparable buddha-qualities, which are uncovered, not produced
pervading all beings as space pervades
not a dependent arising; beyond the three times
possessing the perfections of purity, bliss, self and permanence (RGV 1.35 read as definitive)
negations: empty of the adventitious stains — every conventional phenomenon — which are other than it
not empty of its own nature
not the mere non-affirming negation, the 'emptiness of annihilation' (chad stong) that is nothing whatsoever
relation_to_self: The dharmakāya is the true self in the sense of the perfection of self; the imputed self of persons and phenomena does not exist. Buddha-nature is complete in every being.
relation_to_world: The world of conventional phenomena is empty of its own nature, false and adventitious; it is 'other' than the ultimate, which it obscures but never taints.
caveat: The Jonang affirm one ultimate, but insist that it is other than conventional phenomena and deny that the rangtong emptiness (mere absence of inherent existence) is the final ultimate. The rangtong schools — Gelug (Tsongkhapa, Khedrup), the Sakya scholar Gorampa and many others — reject a non-empty, permanent ultimate as the extreme of eternalism, close to the tīrthikas' self; the Jonang reject the equation of their dharmakāya with a tīrthika ātman. Not yet reconciled: see dsp:rangtong-shentong.

names.name: the Great Mother, Prajñāpāramitā (yum chen mo)
the meaning of the perfection of wisdom (shes rab kyi pha rol tu phyin pa)
Mahāmudrā, the natural state of mind (phyag rgya chen po)

descriptions: the unborn, empty nature of mind in which ego-clinging has been cut
the natural state resting without fixation once the four māras are cut
negations: gods and demons (lha 'dre) have no existence apart from the mind
the self that is clung to has no root
relation_to_self: The self to be cut is ego-clinging (bdag 'dzin); when it is cut, the māras are cut; the Great Mother is the nature of one's own mind.
relation_to_world: Appearances, including terrifying ones, are the display of mind; offered without attachment they become the means of cutting clinging.
caveat: Chöd presents itself as the practice of the Perfection of Wisdom, not as a separate philosophical system; practitioners explain the ultimate according to their own school (rangtong, shentong, Mahāmudrā or Dzogchen). The Great Mother is both the personified deity and emptiness itself.

names.name: the nature of mind, empty and luminous

descriptions: the emptiness whose realization pacifies all suffering
the mind as empty and clear, not to be sought elsewhere
negations: suffering has no ground of its own once its nature is seen
relation_to_self: The self is not found; recognizing the mind's nature ends suffering.
relation_to_world: The world is impermanent and like a dream; attachment to it is to be abandoned.
caveat: Shije is a practice lineage; it does not set out a distinct doctrine of the ultimate beyond the Perfection of Wisdom, and the details of its view survive only in later collections (low confidence).

names.name: selflessness (bdag med), whose non-realization (ignorance) is the root of all disease
the Medicine Buddha (sangs rgyas sman bla), teacher of the Four Tantras

descriptions: the Four Tantras are taught by the Medicine Buddha's emanation of awareness-wisdom (rig pa'i ye shes)
freedom from ignorance is freedom from the root cause of illness
negations: as long as the self is grasped, the causes of disease follow beings as a bird's shadow follows it
relation_to_self: Grasping at a self is the root cause of the three poisons and, through them, of the three nyepa.
relation_to_world: The body and its medicines are composed of the five elements; health belongs to the conventional world and serves Dharma, wealth and happiness.
caveat: Sowa Rigpa is a science (rig gnas), not a philosophical school; it does not posit its own ultimate and defers to Buddhist teaching (Bön physicians to Bön). This entry records only its framing of health and disease within that teaching.

names.name: the Great Madhyamaka (dbu ma chen po), in Kongtrul's presentation
the unity of appearance and emptiness; primordial purity (Mipham)
the single intent (dgongs pa gcig) of the lineages' final views — Dzogchen, Mahāmudrā, Lamdre, the Great Madhyamaka

descriptions: each of the eight practice lineages is a complete path to the same buddhahood
buddha-nature as the union of luminosity and emptiness (Mipham)
the other-empty Great Madhyamaka as the view for meditation, the self-empty Madhyamaka for cutting elaborations in study (Kongtrul, as recalled)
negations: no single school's formulation is the only valid one
the ultimate is neither a mere absence nor a permanent entity (Mipham)
relation_to_self: As in the lineages it preserves: buddha-nature present in all beings; the imputed self does not exist.
relation_to_world: As in the lineages it preserves.
caveat: Rimé is an approach, not a doctrine: its masters insisted that each lineage keep its own view and methods unmixed, and they themselves differed (Kongtrul's shentong-leaning Great Madhyamaka; Mipham's Madhyamaka of unity). Reading it as a single 'one-truth' doctrine would erase the distinctions it insists on. Gelug critics rejected parts of the Rimé masters' views (see dsp:mipham-gelug-madhyamaka).
